paras: The lynching of Bob Young and Charlie Griffin was the hanging of two Black prisoners by a mob of about forty men near La Fayette, Chambers County, Alabama, in August 1882. The two had been convicted of murdering a white man named McCann, but their conviction had been reversed on appeal and a new trial ordered when the mob took them from the jail. Wire reports carried the killing to papers across the country, several of which noted that the men protested their innocence to the end.

Young and Griffin were held at La Fayette on a charge of killing McCann, a killing the Lafayette dispatch placed "some months ago" and the Atlanta dispatch "a year ago." According to the fullest account, the Circuit Court had tried, convicted and sentenced them and fixed a day for their execution, but the Supreme Court reversed the judgment and ordered a new trial. The Lafayette dispatch put it more simply: "The case was still in the courts."

At night a mob of forty men took the two prisoners out of the La Fayette jail by force and carried them out of town. There they hanged both men from an oak tree, and one version of the account adds that the bodies hung there until Sunday morning. Both men, according to the Lafayette wire, protested their innocence to the last.
No member of the mob is named in the coverage, and no report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in it.

The killing reached the press through two separate dispatches: an Atlanta wire dated Aug. 14, printed the next morning in the Savannah Morning News and the New-York Tribune, and a Lafayette, Alabama, wire dated Aug. 15 that ran in western papers from Sacramento to Seattle. Most papers printed one of these as a short telegraphic item, under headlines such as "Hanged by a Mob," "Judge Lynch." and "Colored Men Hung." The Tribune headed the Atlanta version "Two Murderers Lynched," and a Connecticut weekly called the victims "the murderers of Mr. Cann," while the Lafayette wire described them only as arrested for the killing and stressed that the case was still pending.

A longer paragraph in syndicated news summaries, printed in the Huntsville Gazette on Aug. 19 and in Arkansas and Minnesota weeklies the following week, supplied the mob's size, the oak tree and the reversal by the Supreme Court. Copying errors spread with the story: two papers datelined it Lafayette, Indiana, and the names appeared as "Bole" Brooks, "Charla" Griffin, "Griffner," "M. Cann" and "McCam." None of the items located carried editorial comment, and the coverage contains no Black-press report.

The Atlanta wire and the Huntsville Gazette's state-news column date the lynching to Saturday night, Aug. 12, while the Lafayette wire of Aug. 15 says "last night," and a Connecticut brief says Wednesday. Because the Atlanta dispatch was already reporting the lynching on Aug. 14, the Saturday date is the better supported. The first victim is Bob Young in the Lafayette wire and the fuller account but Bob Brooks in the Atlanta wire, and the Huntsville Gazette printed both names in the same issue.

accounts.label: Atlanta wire (Aug. 14)
accounts.gist: On Saturday night in Chambers County a mob lynched Bob Brooks and Charlie Griffin, convicted of murdering McCann a year earlier, who had been granted a new trial.

accounts.label: Lafayette wire (Aug. 15)
accounts.gist: Bob Young and Charlie Griffin, Black men held for the murder of a white man named McCann some months before, were hanged by a mob 'last night' while the case was still in the courts; both protested their innocence.

accounts.label: Syndicated news-summary paragraph
accounts.gist: A mob of forty took the two out of jail by force, carried them out of town and hanged them from an oak after the Supreme Court reversed their conviction; one version adds the bodies hung until Sunday morning.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Lafayette or Atlanta wire as a short telegraphic item under headlines like 'Hanged by a Mob', 'Judge Lynch.' or 'Colored Men Hung', with no comment.

The Atlanta wire's headline in the New-York Tribune called them 'Two Murderers Lynched' and a Connecticut brief 'the murderers of Mr. Cann', while the Lafayette wire noted the case was still in court and that they protested innocence.

conflicts.note: The Atlanta wire was already reporting the lynching on Aug. 14, so the hanging cannot have been the night of Aug. 14 or later; the Alabama state-news column's 'on the 12th' agrees with Saturday, Aug. 12.
Same pair, county, charge and new trial; the first man's surname differs between the Lafayette and Atlanta wires, and the Huntsville Gazette printed both in one issue.
The Indiana dateline is an error on copies of the same wire text.
